translations.text: He had a stern mind; grimly angered, he seized them in wrath with hostile hands and, furious at heart, broke them in his grip. The noble one cut his adversaries off from their glorious dwellings.
The Ruler sent the hateful host on a long journey, those sad spirits. Their boast was crushed, their vow shattered, and their power brought low, their beauty defiled.
Then there was truly peace in heaven as before, fair customs of peace. The Lord was dear to all, the prince to his thanes. The glories of the hosts who possessed joy with the Lord increased.

Those who dwell in the sky, the homeland of glory, were then in harmony. Strife had ended, and so had terror and warlike hatred among the angels, since the warmongers had left heaven, deprived of light.
The flood was divided by holy powers under the high firmament, water from the waters that still remain under the stronghold, the roof of the peoples.
Then the guardian of life, the shepherd of hosts, saw dry land, widely revealed, when the King of glory named it earth.

Then he spoke these words: "Be fruitful now and increase. Fill the all-green earth with offspring, with your kin, sons and daughters. The salt water and all the creation of the world shall remain in the power of you two.

Enjoy the days of plenty, and the burden of the sea, and the birds of heaven. To you two are given into your power the holy livestock and the wild beasts, and the living things that tread the land, the kinds endowed with life, and those that the flood brings forth throughout the whale-road. All things obey you."
Then, by the Lord's powers, all were divided out of one when he created this earth, with water of bright beauty, and he sent them out into the world.
People, the dwellers on earth, call one of these the Pishon. With its bright streams it encircles that part of the land, Havilah, broadly from outside.
In that homeland, as books tell us, the children of the nations of men find gold and gems, the best of them, near and far.
Then the second river surrounds from outside the land and dwelling-place of the people of Ethiopia, a spacious kingdom. Its name is Gihon.
…highest next to himself in the kingdom of heaven. He had made him so bright, and so lovely was the form that came to him in heaven from the Lord of hosts, that he was like the bright stars.
The angel of pride spoke many words. He thought about how, by his own strength alone, he might make himself a stronger throne, higher in the heavens.
He said that his mind urged him to begin building in the west and north and to set up structures. He said he doubted that he would remain God's subordinate.
"Why should I toil?" he said. "I have no need at all to have a master. I can work as many wonders with my own hands.
…he had to pay for that deed and take his share of the pain of that strife, and he had to have his punishment, the greatest of all torments.
So does every man who begins to strive wickedly against his Ruler, against the glorious Lord. Then the Mighty One, the highest Ruler of heaven, became enraged and threw him down from the high throne.
Then he cut him off from his favour and threw him into hell, into the deep pits, where he became a devil, the fiend together with all his companions.
Then the angels fell from heaven above, for as long as three nights and days, from heaven into hell, and the Lord changed them all into devils.
Because they would not honour his deed and word, almighty God therefore set them, without victory, in a worse light down beneath the earth, in the black hell.

There, in the evening, each and every one of the fiends has fire renewed for an immeasurably long time; then at dawn comes the east wind, frost fiercely cold. Always fire or piercing cold [?]: they had to endure some hard torment.

It was made for them as a punishment (their world was overturned): for the first time he filled hell with the adversaries. From then on the angels who had kept God's favour before held the heights of the kingdom of heaven.
The other fiends, who had earlier waged so much strife against their Ruler, lay in the fire.
They suffer torment, hot surging fire in the midst of hell, burning and broad flames, and likewise the bitter smoke, fumes and darkness, because they neglected the service of God.
Their wantonness deceived them, the angel's pride; they would not honour the word of the All-Ruler; they had great torment.

Then, because of their folly and their pride, they had fallen through fire to the bottom, into hot hell. They had come to another land, one that was without light and full of flame, a great terror of fire.
The fiends perceived that they had received in exchange countless torments through their great presumption and through the might of God, and most of all through their arrogance.

Then the proud king spoke, he who had once been the most beautiful of angels, the brightest in heaven, beloved of his Master and dear to the Lord, until they turned to folly, so that God himself, mighty in mind, became angry with him for his arrogance.

He threw him into that destruction, down into that bed of death, and afterwards gave him a name: the Highest said that from then on he should be called Satan. He commanded him to keep watch over the abyss of the black hell, and not to strive against God.
Satan spoke; sorrowing he said, he who from then on was to hold hell and keep watch over the abyss:
He had once been God's angel, bright in heaven, until his mind and, most of all, his pride led him astray, so that he would not honour the word of the Lord of hosts.
His thoughts welled up within him around his heart, and outside him was hot and cruel punishment. Then he spoke these words:

"This narrow place is very unlike the other home that we knew before, high in the kingdom of heaven, which my Lord granted me, though because of the All-Ruler we were not allowed to possess it or to extend [?] our realm.
Yet he has not done right in casting us down to the bottom of the fire, of the hot hell, deprived of the kingdom of heaven. He has marked it out to be settled with mankind.
That is the greatest of sorrows to me: that Adam, who was made of earth, shall hold my mighty throne and live in joy, while we suffer this torment, this harm in this hell.
Alas! If I had the power of my hands and could get out for one hour, be out for one winter's hour, then I with this host— But iron bonds lie about me, the rope of chain rides me.
I am stripped of my kingdom. The fetters of hell have seized me so hard and hold me fast. Here is a great fire, above and below. I never saw a more hateful landscape.
The flame does not die down, hot over hell. The clasp of rings, the cruelly hard rope, has kept me from moving and taken away my going; my feet are bound, my hands fettered.
The ways out through these doors of hell are blocked, so that I cannot by any means get free of these limb-bonds. Great bars of hard iron, forged hot, lie about me.

For God has fettered me by the neck, and so I know that he knew my mind. The Lord of hosts also knew that things would go badly between Adam and me over the heavenly kingdom if I had the use of my hands.
But now we suffer torments in hell (they are darkness and heat), grim and bottomless. God himself has swept us into these dark mists.
Although he cannot charge us with any sin, any harm we did him in that land, he has still cut us off from the light and cast us into the greatest of all torments.
We cannot take vengeance for this, or repay him with any harm because he has cut us off from the light.
He has now marked out a middle-earth, where he has made man after his likeness. With him he means to fill the kingdom of heaven again with pure souls.
So we must think hard about how we may avenge our grievance on Adam, if we ever can, and on his offspring as well, and turn them away from his will there, if we can devise it in any way.
I no longer hope for that light which he thinks to enjoy for a long time, that bliss with the strength of his angels. We can never achieve it, that we should weaken the mind of mighty God.

Let us now turn it away from the children of men, that kingdom of heaven, now that we may not have it; let us bring it about that they give up his favour, so that they overturn what he commanded with his word.
then he will grow angry with them in his mind and cast them out of his favour. Then they will have to come to this hell and these grim depths.
Then we can have them as our servants, the children of men, in these fast fetters. Now begin to think about the expedition!
If in former days I ever gave princely treasures to any thane while we sat happy in that good kingdom and held our thrones, then he could never repay my gifts at a more welcome time,
if any of my thanes would still agree to it, so that he could come up and out of here through these prison bars, and had the power in him to fly with a feather-coat,
than by flying up through the sky to where Adam and Eve stand, created, in the earthly kingdom, surrounded by riches, while we are cast down here into these deep valleys.

Now they are far more precious to the Lord, and they may possess the wealth that we should have had in the kingdom of heaven, the realm that was ours by right. That gift has been allotted to the race of men.
It is so painful to me in my mind, and it grieves me in my heart, that they are to possess the kingdom of heaven forever.
If any of you can bring it about in any way that they abandon God's word and his teaching, they will soon become more hateful to him.
If they break his command, then he will become enraged with them. After that their prosperity will be taken away, and punishment will be prepared for them, some harsh and grievous fate.
All of you, think about how you might deceive them! Then I can rest easy in these chains, if they lose that kingdom.
Whoever accomplishes this will have a reward ready for him afterwards forever, from whatever benefits we can win in here, in this fire, from now on.
I will let him sit beside me, whoever comes into this hot hell to tell me that they have [?] the heavenly King's teaching unworthily in words and deeds." Then God's adversary began to equip himself.
eager in his gear (he had a treacherous mind), he set a helmet of concealment on his head and bound it very tightly, fastening it with clasps. He knew many speeches of crooked [?] words.
He swung up from there and went through the doors of hell (he had a strong mind). Hostile in mind, he flew through the air and split the fire in two with a fiend's power.
He wanted to deceive the Lord's followers, the humans, in secret with wicked deeds, and to mislead and lead them astray so that they became hateful to God.

He then travelled by a fiend's power until he found Adam on earth, God's handiwork, ready and wisely made, and with him his wife, the fairest woman, as they knew how to do much good [?], whom the Lord of mankind had himself marked out as his servants.
And beside them stood two trees, laden on the outside with fruit and covered in produce, just as the ruling God, the high King of heaven, had set them there with his hands,
so that there the children of men, every one of them, could choose between good and evil, prosperity and woe. The fruit of the two trees was not alike!

The one was so pleasant, beautiful and bright, gentle and praiseworthy: that was the tree of life. Whoever bit into that fruit could live on afterwards into eternity and remain in the world, so that old age would not harm him after that,

nor grievous sickness. Instead he could always live straight away in delights and keep his life and the favour of the King of heaven here in the world, and have, as a pledge, the honours appointed to him in high heaven when he departed from here.

The other tree was entirely black, dim and dark: that was the tree of death, which bore much bitterness. Every man who ate of it would have to know both evil and good, the difference between them in this world.
Whoever tasted what grew on that tree would have to live ever afterwards in punishment, with sweat and with sorrows.
Old age was to take from him his deeds of courage, his joys and his lordship, and death was to be allotted to him.
He would enjoy his life for only a little while, and then go to the blackest of lands, in fire.
He would have to serve fiends, where the greatest of all dangers lies for people for a long time. The hateful one knew that well, the devil's secret messenger, who had fought against the Lord.

Then by the devil's power he took on the body of a serpent and wound himself around the tree of death. He took some of the fruit there and turned back from there to where he knew the handiwork of the King of heaven was.
Then the hateful one, full of lies, began to question him with his first words: "Adam, do you long for anything up there with God?
I have travelled here from far away on his errand, and it was not long ago that I sat beside him.

Then he ordered me to go on this journey. He ordered that you eat this fruit, and said that your strength and skill and your understanding would become greater, and your body much brighter, and your form more beautiful. He said that you would never need any wealth in the world.

"I do not know whether you come with lies out of some secret purpose, or whether you are the Lord's messenger from heaven. I cannot understand anything of your commands, your words or your ways, your journey or your sayings.
You are not like any of his angels that I have seen before, and you have not shown me any token that my lord sent me in faith and grace.
"But I know all the orders of angels and the high vaults of the heavens very well. I served God eagerly for a long time with a loyal mind, my Lord, the Lord himself. I am not like a devil."

but the enemy worked hard to deceive the soul to whom he had earlier lent that sight, so that she could look so far across the heavenly kingdom. Then the accursed one spoke out of enmity (he did not advise them for their good at all):
Full woe is the man who does not guard himself while he has the power to!
Then the one who was hateful to God led her astray with lies, out of hatred for the heavenly King. He seduced Eve's mind, the weak thought of a woman, so that she began to trust his words,
If you said anything harmful to him today, he will still forgive it, if we two are willing to serve him.

I can hear far and wide, and see so widely over all the world, over this broad creation; I can hear the joy of heaven in the heavens. It has grown light in my mind, outside and inside, since I bit into the fruit.
It is not like anything else on earth, except as this messenger says: that it came directly from God."
The hostile messenger stood there, laid desires upon him and enticed him with cunning, pressed after him boldly. The fiend who had made that perilous expedition over a long road was very near.

Yet she did it with a loyal heart. She did not know that so many harms and terrible afflictions would follow for mankind because she took it into her mind to listen to the teachings of the hateful messenger.
Therefore my mind is healed, and my spirit is at ease around my heart. All our harms are avenged, the injury that we two have long suffered.

The two of them, Adam and Eve, grieved, and they often exchanged words of lament between them. They feared God, their lord's hatred; they greatly dreaded the enmity of the King of heaven. They themselves understood that his word had been overturned.

The woman mourned and lamented, sorrowful in mind (she had forsaken God's favour and his teaching), when she saw that light glide away elsewhere, the light that he who had counselled them to that injury had shown her as a sign of faithlessness,
so that they would have to suffer the hostility of hell, countless humiliations; therefore sorrows of mind burned in their breasts.

At times the married pair fell to prayer together, and they hailed the good Lord of victory and called on God, the Ruler of heaven, and asked him that they might take his punishment and eagerly carry it out in full, since they had broken God's command.

They saw that their bodies were bare. In that land they did not yet have settled dwellings, nor did they know any of the sorrow of labour; they could have lived well in that land if they had been willing to carry out God's teaching continually.
Then they spoke many sorrowful words together, the married pair, the two of them.
Adam spoke and said to Eve: "Lo, Eve, you have marked out an evil fate for the two of us.
Do you see now the dark hell, greedy and ravenous? Now you can hear it raging from here.

The kingdom of heaven is not like that fire. But this is the best of lands, which we two might have kept by our Lord's grace if you had not listened to the one who counselled us to this harm, so that we broke the word of the Ruler, the King of heaven.
Now we two, sorrowful, may grieve for this fate. For he himself commanded us to guard ourselves against punishment, the greatest of harms.
Now hunger and thirst tear at me bitterly in my breast, though before we were both free of these cares at all times.
How shall we two live now, or survive in this land, if the wind comes here from west or east, south or north?
Dark cloud rises up, a shower of hail comes pressing down from heaven, and frost comes along with it, terribly cold.
At times the heavens shine hot, this bright sun blazes, and we two stand here naked, with no clothing to protect us.
We have nothing in front of us as shelter from the storms, and nothing set aside for food. Instead the mighty God, the Ruler, is angry with us. What will become of us now?
Now I may regret that I asked the God of heaven, the good Ruler, to make you here for me from my own limbs, now that you have led me astray into my Lord's hatred.
So now I may regret for ever and ever that I ever saw you with my eyes."
Then Eve spoke in turn, the fairest of women, the most beautiful of wives. She was God's handiwork, though she had then been deceived by the devil's craft:
"You may blame me for it with your words, my dear Adam. Yet it cannot grieve you any worse in your mind than it grieves me in my heart."

Then Adam answered her: "If I knew the Ruler's will, and what punishment I must take from him, you would never see anything quicker than I would be, even if the God of heaven commanded me to wade into the sea from here right now, [?]
…to travel on the flood, were it ever so terribly deep, the sea-stream ever so great, that my mind would never doubt it [?], but I would go to the very bottom, if I could carry out God's will.
I have no need in the world of any service, now that I have lost my Lord's favour, so that I cannot have it.
But we two cannot stay here naked together like this to any purpose. Let us go into this forest, into the shelter of this wood."

The two of them turned and went away mourning into the green forest. They sat apart and waited for their fate from the King of heaven himself, since they could no longer have what almighty God had given them before.
Then they covered their bodies with leaves and clothed themselves with the forest, since they had no garments.

…but they fell to prayer, both of them together, every morning. They prayed the Mighty One, God almighty, not to forget them, and prayed that the good Ruler would guide them in how they should live from then on in that light.

Then the Lord almighty, the glorious Prince, came walking into Paradise after midday, for his own purpose. Our Saviour, the merciful Father, wished to see what his children were doing. He knew that those to whom he had once given beauty had fallen into sin.
Then they went off, sad at heart, under the shade of the trees, robbed of their glory. They hid themselves in darkness when they heard the holy word of the Lord, and they were afraid.
Then at once the Prince of the heavens, the Guardian, began to question the creatures of the world. The mighty Prince ordered his son to come to him quickly.
Then almighty God asked Eve about it: "What have you done, daughter, with the plentiful benefits, the new creations of paradise, the growing gifts,

Behind them, at the Lord's command, a holy angel locked with a fiery sword the hopeful home of comforts and joys. No man full of malice and stained with sin may go there, for the guardian, who keeps that glorious life, precious in its blessings, for the Lord, has might and strength.
He commanded sea and earth to bring forth fruits for the married couple, for every family of the offspring-bearing creatures, for use in the world.
Then, at God's command, they began to beget children, as the Creator had commanded them.
One of them, the firstborn, worked the earth with vigour; the other kept livestock to help his father, until a great number of days had passed.
Then they both brought offerings to the Lord. The Prince of angels, the King of all creatures, looked with his eyes on Abel's offering; he would not look at Cain's sacrifice.
That was a grief to the man, heavy at his heart. A surge of passion rose up in the man's breast: livid hatred, anger out of envy.
Then with his hands he did a wicked deed: Cain slew his kinsman, his brother Abel, and shed his blood. The earth swallowed that slaughter-blood, the man's gore.
After the deadly blow, woe was raised up, an offspring of sorrows. From that branch hateful, cruel fruits afterwards grew, more and more strongly the longer it went on.
Then the wicked worker of death answered him at once: "I do not know Abel's coming or going, my kinsman's journey, nor was I my brother's keeper."
You shall wander in sorrow, without honour, away from your homeland, because you became Abel's slayer. Therefore you must travel far-wandering paths as an outcast, hateful to your kinsmen."

The Ruler, the glorious Measurer, the Lord, set a token on him, a sign of protection, so that none of his enemies would dare to attack him with violence in battle, from far or near. Then he commanded the guilty man to go away from his mother and kinsmen, from his own kindred.
The eldest was called Jared, son of Enos. After that the family of Cain arose, those who increased the generations of that race.
Afterwards Methuselah shared out the princes' treasure to his kinsmen, child after child, to his brothers, until, old and full of years, he had to meet his parting from life and give up his life.
I have stained my hands with the killing of Cain. With my hands I struck down the father of Enos, the first slayer of Abel, and gave the man's slaughter-blood to the earth.
I know well that after this killing will come the sevenfold vengeance of the true King, great after the crime. My fall and death will be repaid more severely, with grim terror, when I go forth."

Writings tell us that here on earth Adam afterwards increased his family with women and men for eight hundred [years]. In all he had lived nine hundred and [?] winters when he had to give up this world through the parting of the soul.

After him Seth ruled the people, the son after his parents. He held the ancestral seat and took a wife. He was a hundred and five winters old when he first began to increase the people of his family with sons and daughters.
After him Mahalalel held the land and inheritance for many half-years.
He lived in the kingdom of the world for a hundred and five winters, and sixty more, before the time came when his wife brought a son into the world. The son was called Enoch, a noble firstborn.
From here that man went in his body to seek grace, the company of the Lord. He did not die the death of middle-earth at all, as men here do, young and old,

when God takes from them their possessions and sustenance, the treasures of the earth, and their life with them. Instead he departed alive with the King of angels from this passing life, to travel in the garments his spirit had received before his mother brought him into the world of men.
He named the eldest Noah, who ruled the land among men after Lamech passed away.

After that, for a hundred and twenty winters by count, the doomed peoples busied themselves with wickedness in the world, until the Lord chose to inflict punishment on the oath-breakers and strike dead the giants, who were guilty in their deeds, unloved by God, great evildoers, hateful to the Measurer.
Then the Ruler, our Saviour, spoke and said to Noah: "I will destroy the people with a flood, along with every kind of living creature that air and water bring forth and feed, cattle and birds.
You will have protection with your sons when the black water, the dark streams of death, swallow up the hosts, the guilty wrongdoers.
Build that vessel fifty ells wide, thirty high and three hundred long, and build it to withstand the waves, joining it firmly together.
He told his kinsmen that a dreadful thing was coming upon the peoples, a cruel punishment. They paid no attention to it!

Then our Saviour said to Noah: "Dearest of men, I give you my pledge of this: that you will set out on your way, carrying the offspring of the living creatures you must bring, over the deep water for a great number of days in the ship's hold.
Feed the offspring of living creatures generously until, after the sea-voyage, I choose to make room again under the heavens for food for the survivors.
Go now with your household into that dwelling, with the company of souls. I know you to be good and steadfast of mind; you are worthy of protection and of mercy, together with your children.
Now, after seven nights, I will let deadly rain fall from above onto the face of the wide earth.

For forty days I will bring hostility on men, and with a host of waves I will destroy all possessions and their owners that are outside the boards of the ark when the black storm-cloud begins to rise."
Then Noah went, as the Saviour commanded him, to lead his sons under the deck of the ark, the men onto the ship, and their wives with them;
and everything that the Lord Almighty wished to have for breeding went under the roof to the one who would feed them, as the Almighty Lord of hosts had commanded him by his word.
Behind him the Guardian of the heavenly kingdom, the Ruler of victories, closed the door of the sea-house with his own hands, and our Saviour blessed the inside of the ark with his own powers.
Noah, son of Lamech, was six hundred winters old when he went on board with his children, wise with the young ones, at God's command, with his dear company.
The Lord sent rain from the heavens, and he also let springs pour abundantly into the world from every vein, and let dark ocean-streams roar. The seas rose up over the shore-walls.

Strong and fierce was he who ruled the waters. Because of their wicked enmity he covered and roofed over the children of the earth with the dark wave, over the homeland of men. He ravaged their dwellings; the Ruler avenged on men the injury done to his heart.

The sea gripped the doomed people hard for forty days and as many nights. The punishment was fierce, deadly and grim to men. The waves of the King of glory drove the life of the wicked out of their bodies.

The flood, rough beneath the heavens, covered all the high mountains across the wide earth. It lifted the ark up from the earth onto the water, and with it the noble ones whom the Lord himself, our Creator, had blessed when he shut up that ship.

After that the best of dwellings rode far and wide under the clouds over the ring of the sea and travelled with its cargo. The terrors of the water could not strike violently at the seafarers with sudden danger, for holy God carried them and saved them.
The drowning flood stood fifteen ells deep, by a man's measure, over the hills. That is a famous event!
In the end there was nothing to separate them, except that heaven was raised up into the high air, when the ocean-host had killed all the offspring of the earth.
except that the Lord of the heavens held up the ark's timbers, when holy God, the eternal one, the stern-hearted King, let the flood climb up in its streams and lifted it up, humble [?].
Then God, the Ruler of victories, the source of the light of life, remembered the seafarer, the son of Lamech, and all the offspring he had shut in against the water in the ship's bosom.

Then the Lord of hosts guided the warrior by his word over the wide land. The surging flood began to lessen again. The water ebbed, dark beneath the sky. The true Ruler had turned the ocean-stream back for the children, back to its bright course, and had stilled the rain.

The foaming ship travelled a hundred and fifty nights under the heavens after the flood lifted up the nail-boarded vessel, the best of ships, until the counted number of days of that fierce time had passed.
Then the greatest of sea-houses, Noah's ark, came to rest high with its cargo on the mountains that are called Armenia.

There the holy one, the son of Lamech, waited a long time for the true promises to be fulfilled, waiting for when the Guardian of life, the Lord Almighty, would give him rest from his perilous journeys. He had endured them far and wide when the dark waves carried him on the sea across the wide earth.

The sea was going down. The men, the seafarers, and their wives as well, longed for the time when they might step out of their confinement over the nail-boarded side onto the shore and lead their possessions out of that narrow place.
Then the ship's captain tested whether the sinking sea-flood still lay beneath the clouds.
Then, many days after the high slopes had received the treasure, and also the noble ones of the earth's offspring, the son of Lamech let a black raven fly out of the house over the deep flood.

Noah reckoned that if the raven found no land on that journey, it would have to seek him out again over the wide water on the ship. But that hope deceived him, for the bird perched gleefully on a floating corpse; the dark-feathered one would not seek him.
She shook her feathers and went flying back with her gift. The flier brought a single twig of an olive tree to his hands, with green leaves.

Then our Saviour, the Guardian of the kingdom of heaven, spoke to Noah with holy voice: "A homeland is opened to you again, a pleasant place on land, rest from voyages on the water, fair upon the earth.

Go out in peace from the ark, and from the high dwelling lead your household onto the bosom of the earth, and all the offspring that I saved on the ship in the distress of the waves, while the water had covered the third homeland with its might."
He did so and obeyed the Lord. With great joy he climbed over the ship's side, as the voice commanded him, and led out of the wave-ship the remnant left from the wrath.
You may often and frequently see a sign of this in the clouds, when I show my rainbow, that I keep this covenant with men as long as the world stands."

Then Noah began anew to establish a home with his kinsmen and to till food for them from the earth. He toiled and worked, planted a vineyard, sowed many seeds, and eagerly sought what the green earth brought him: bright, beautiful fruits, splendid gifts.

That was painful in mind to the holy man. He then began to curse his own son with words, and said that Ham must be lowly under the heavens, a servant of his kinsmen on earth. That sentence afterwards harmed him and his descendants terribly.
Then the offspring of Japheth was raised, a joyful household of close kinsmen, sons and daughters.
after they sought out the plain of Shinar, as the very mighty leaders of the people, the eldest, often and frequently dwelt there pleasantly;

[?] …by counsels the men turned to work and to wrongdoing, until in their pride and folly they showed their skill: they built a city and raised a ladder up to the heavens, and with their strength they put up a stone wall beyond the measure of men. They were eager for glory, those men, with their hands.
Then holy God came to look at the work of the generations of men, the fortified city of men, and also the tower which the children of Adam had begun to raise up to the heavens,
And the stern-hearted King punished that folly when, fierce of mood, he made the speech of the earth-dwellers unlike, so that their speech did not succeed for them.
When they met in bands at the tower, strong in might and in great numbers, for the business of the work, none of the tribes of men there knew what another said.

They could not build the stone wall any higher, but wretchedly broke apart in bands, divided by their speech. Each kin group had become foreign to the others, after the Creator, through the abundance of his might, scattered the speech of men.
Then the sons of nobles went apart along four ways, divided, in search of land. Behind them both the strong stone tower and the steep city stood together, half-built, in Shinar.
Then the kin of Shem grew and flourished under the clouds, until a man was born in that line, among the number of royal children, a thoughtful man, mindful of virtues.

Sons were born to the nobleman, two noble children brought up in Babylon. Those chieftains, bold-minded men, were called Abraham and Haran. The Lord of angels was friend and lord to both of those men.
Then a son was brought up to Haran, beloved in life, whose name was Lot.

Those young men, Abraham and Lot, prospered before the Lord without reproach, as their nobility in the kingdom of the world had come from their forefathers. For this reason the children of noble nations now honour them far and wide with glory.
When the appointed time had come, Abraham brought a lady home as his wife, to where he had his dwelling, fair and noble. The woman was called Sarah, as books tell us.
Then for many winters they shared the world and their treasure together, and kept peace for a great number of years.
Yet it was still not granted to Abraham that the beautiful lady, Sarah, should bring into the world an heir for him, sons and daughters for Abraham.
Then Abraham's father set out with his family, journeying with provisions across the people of the Chaldeans. Wise, with his kinsmen, he wanted to seek the land of Canaan.
His kinsmen, chosen by the Lord, Abraham and Lot, journeyed with him from that homeland.
Then the noble sons of princes, men with their wives, took a dwelling place in Haran. In those dwellings Abraham's father, a faithful man, gave up his life;
he had two hundred and five winters, counted by number, when he departed, old in years, to see the Lord's decree.

Then the Holy One, the Guardian of the kingdom of heaven, the eternal Lord, spoke to Abraham: "Go now, journey forth and lead your company and your possessions with your family. Leave Haran, your father's homeland.
Go as I command you, dearest of men, and obey my teachings well, and seek the land that I will show you, all green, the broad earth. You shall live blessed under my protection.
If any dweller on earth greets you with woe, I will set my curse on him, and fierce anger, long-lasting enmity. I will give grace, the fruit of their desires, to those who honour you.
Through you all dwellers on earth, the children of the peoples, shall receive peace and friendship, my joy and blessing in the kingdom of the world."
"The number of your kin shall flourish greatly under heaven, in sons and daughters, until the earth becomes [full of] your offspring, and many a nation is filled with your descendants."

Then Abraham departed, leading his possessions out of the borders of Egypt. He was good in noble virtues, very rich in gold and silver, and blessed. As the Guardian of victories, our Ruler, commanded him through his word, he led his cattle from Haran. They sought the land of Canaan and the dwelling place of the people.

Then the one dear to God came into that homeland, leading the women, his beloved bedfellow and his nephew's wife, as he wished. He was seventy-five winters old when he had to set out and leave Haran and his kinsmen.

Then Abraham went journeying, mindful of the teaching of the Father almighty, to view the land far and wide throughout the nations at the Lord's command, until the courageous man, successful in his journey, came to Shechem, to the race of the Canaanites.

Then the King of angels himself appeared to Abraham, the glorious one of hosts, and the Lord said: "This is the land, all green, bright and rich with fruits, that I will give into the power of your offspring, a spacious kingdom."
Then the man built an altar to God and offered a sacrifice to the Ruler of life, the Source of light, the Protector of souls.

Then Abraham went on from the east to look with his eyes on the choicest of lands. (He remembered the grace of heaven's Guardian's promise, when the King of victories himself had revealed the truth to him through holy word.) He went until the lordly men came with their company to where the rich dwelling place called Bethlehem is.

The man, glad at heart, and his brother's son, devout men, travelled on from the east with their possessions through famous lands and slopes steep as walls. They chose dwellings for themselves where the plains seemed beautiful to them.

They made it known to their lord of the people that few women were fairer [?] before the prince, but they praised Sarah far more, her winsome beauty, with words, until he commanded the lovely woman to be led to his own hall.

There the blessed man once again honoured the name of the eternal Lord with a new voice; the good-minded man offered a sacrifice to the Lord of angels and thanked the Source of the light of life greatly for his favours and mercies.

Then the son of Haran chose for himself a dwelling and a home in the city of Sodom; he led away all his possessions, rings from Bethlehem and household treasures, wealth, twisted gold. Afterward he lived by the Jordan for many years.
The people of Sodom were bold in sins and perverse in deeds; they brought about their own eternal ruin.
Lot would never adopt the customs of that people, but he shunned the ways of that tribe, their deceit and crime, though he had to live in that land,
Then the four kings of nations set out from there with a great force, going south to attack Sodom and Gomorrah.

Then the homeland of the men by the Jordan was overrun far and wide by war-bands, the land by enemies. Many a frightened, pale-cheeked woman had to go trembling into a stranger's embrace; the defenders of brides and rings fell, sick with wounds.

For twelve winters before this they had been forced to pay tribute to the northern men and to give taxes, until the people would no longer strengthen the prince of the Elamites with the people's treasures, but revolted from him.
There was hard play, an exchange of deadly spears, a great war-clamour, a loud sound of battle. Warriors drew ring-marked swords, strong of edge, from their sheaths with their hands.
The leader of the Elamites won the victory in war and held the field of slaughter. Those left alive by the weapons went to seek a stronghold.
The men were brave; they carried their shields boldly forward along the road.
He said that the holy, eternal Lord could easily grant him success in that spear-strife.
Behind him stood a joyful hearth-troop, and the warriors lay, sat [?] on the track, those who had robbed Sodom and Gomorrah of gold and plundered them [?] (stigwitum).
Then Abraham went to see the retreat of the hateful men along the battle-road. Lot was rescued, the nobleman with his possessions; the women returned, wives as they wished.

Far and wide they saw birds tearing the slayers of free men amid the sword-slaughter. Abraham brought treasure and brides back to the men of the south, the children of nobles, nearer to their homeland, maidens to their kinsmen.

"Give me the servants of my people, whom you rescued by the strength of your army from the deadly grip of men! Keep for yourself the twisted gold that once belonged to our people, the wealth and treasures!
Let me lead the children of nobles back, free, to their homeland, to their desolate dwellings: women and boys, poor widows!
The sons are dead, the companions of the people, except for a few alone, who were to guard the borders with me."
Then the ruler set out on his journey home with the plunder that the holy man had given him, the man of the Hebrews, mindful of honours.

Then once again the high King of the heavens himself spoke holy words to Abraham, encouraged the good-minded man and said to him: "Your rewards are great! Do not let your spirit grow slack, you who are steadfast in my will!
"My steward goes about glad with his freeborn children; he firmly intends in his thoughts that his sons shall be my heirs after me."
"A son will yet be born to you, a child come from your bride by birth, who will afterward be the guardian of the inheritance, famous before God. Do not mourn!
I am the Ruler who many winters ago led you out of the city of the Chaldeans, as one of four, and promised you wide dwelling-places to rule over.

"Now, kinsman of the Hebrews, I give you my covenant: your land shall be settled with your offspring, many a broad land, the regions of the earth as far as the Euphrates, and from the borders of the Egyptians, as far among men as the Nile divides, and again to the Mediterranean, a wide kingdom.
Your descendants shall own all of that, every one of the nations, as far as the three waters, the foaming floods, wind their streams around the high stone cities, the dwelling-places of the peoples."
Then Sarah was sore at heart that no child had been born to her and Abraham together through their sharing a bed, a noble child to comfort them.
"Go quickly to her bed, then, and find out whether the Lord will let any heir of yours come into the world through that woman."
Then the blessed man agreed to the woman's counsel. As his wife advised, he told the serving-woman to go to bed with him.
"Hagar shall pay for that, if you let me rule my own servant, dear Abraham. May the Almighty, Lord of lords, judge this between the two of us."
The wise-minded man answered her at once with his words: "I will not leave you without honour while we both live. You may treat your own serving-woman as your heart pleases."
"Now I must wait in the wilderness with tears on my cheeks for my fate, until hunger or the wolf tears soul and sorrow together from my heart."
"Hagar, you shall bring a son into the world for Abraham. With these words of mine I tell you now that the boy shall be called Ishmael among men.
He will be fierce and eager for battle, an enemy to the families of men, to his own kin. Many will fight against him in anger with violent weapons.
From that founder peoples will spring, a countless nation. Go back now to your master; stay with those who own you!"
Then Ishmael was born to Abraham, just when he had lived eighty-six winters in the world.
The son grew and thrived, as the angel, the faithful messenger of peace, had told the woman in his own words.
Then after thirteen years the Prince, the eternal Lord, spoke with Abraham: "Beloved, keep our covenant well, as I instruct you!

I will raise you up in prosperity at all times. Be firm in doing my will! From now on I will faithfully keep the covenant that I gave you long ago as a pledge of comfort, for which your spirit had mourned.
"You shall sanctify your household.
Set the true sign of victory on every male, if you want to have in me a lord or a loyal friend to your offspring.
I will be the shepherd and guardian of that people, if you obey me in the thoughts of your hearts and are willing to fulfil my commands.

Every male of that lineage who comes into the world shall be dedicated to me as a child after seven nights with the sign of victory, or else be cut off far from the earth in enmity and driven from all good things. Do as I command!"
I will keep faith with you, if you take on that sign of true faith. You shall have a son, a child by your wife, whom all the city-dwellers shall call Isaac.
You need not be ashamed of that heir. Rather, I will give that young man my divine grace through the powers of the spirit, an abundance of friends, along with benefits.

He shall receive my bliss and blessing, love and favour. From that founder of the people a broad nation shall come. Many lords shall rise up valiant, guardians of the kingdom, kings of the world, widely famous."
Abraham then quickly laid his face on the ground, and in his heart and mind he turned the spoken words over with scorn.

Abraham himself did not expect from that day's speech that Sarah, his grey-haired wife, could bring a son into the world. He knew well that the woman had indeed reached a full hundred winters, counted by number.

Then, old in years, he answered the Creator: "Likewise may Ishmael live by your teachings, Lord, and bear you thanks, a resolute mind and a strong heart, to carry out your will day and night in words and deeds."
Then the almighty Lord, the eternal Lord, answered him graciously: "Sarah, old in winters, shall bring a son into the world for you. Truly, events shall go forward according to these spoken terms.

I will gladly bless Ishmael now, as you are asking for your firstborn, so that he may live to see many days of life in the kingdom of the world, with branches of offspring. Let that be granted to you!

Yet I will raise up more greatly Isaac, your heir, the young child who has not yet come into the world, with abundant goods and every excellence in his days. I will truly keep with him my covenant of the mind, holy and faithful intentions, and I will be gracious to him."
Abraham did as the Eternal had commanded him. At the Lord's bidding he set the sign of peace upon his own son, and ordered every high-ranking man to bear that sign,
[?] who was of his household, of the male kind. Mindful of the covenant and wise in mind, when God gave him true pledges, he then received the bright sign himself.

The Creator, the glorious King, ever increased his fame with excellences in the kingdom of the world. Abraham had earned this from him, since from the very first on his journey he was able to carry out his Ruler's will.

Then the woman laughed at the Lord of hosts, not at all gladly. Old in years, she mocked that spoken promise bitterly in her mind. She did not believe the truth, that fulfilment would follow that speech.
When the Ruler of the heavens heard that Abraham's wife had raised hopeless laughter in the chamber, holy God said: "Sarah will not believe the truth of my words.
Yet fate shall go forward just as I promised you at the beginning.
I tell you truly: at this same time an heir will be born of the woman.
When I visit this same dwelling a second time, my promises to you will be fulfilled. You will look on a son, your own child, dear Abraham!"

After that speech the holy spirits, eager to go elsewhere, quickly set out from the place of speaking and travelled with speed. They left their tracks behind them, and Lot's kinsman himself went with them as a companion, until they could look upon Sodom, the steep-walled city.
They saw halls towering over treasure, buildings over red gold. Then the Ruler of the skies, gracious to Abraham, began to speak and told him no small news:

"In this city I hear an uproar, the very loud cry of sinners, the boasting of the ale-merry. The crowd within the walls uses evil speech. Therefore the sins of the people, the oath-breakers, are heavy.
"Kinsman of the Hebrews, I will now find out what those men are doing, whether they commit sins as greatly in their habits and thoughts as they perversely speak deceit and malice;

Proud in their prosperity, they repaid the Lord's goodness with wickedness, until the Protector of spirits, the source of the light of life, would no longer endure the offence. The stern-minded King sent two strong messengers of his to them, and at eventide they made their way to the city of Sodom.
There the noble, wise-minded man gave them fine hospitality in his hall, until the evening light had gone.
Then night came, following on the heels of day. With darkness it covered the ocean streams, the splendour of this life, the seas and the broad lands.
"I know a high city near here, a little town. Grant me mercy and rest there, so that we may go up to Zoar to seek refuge for our lives."
Ever after, the image (that is a famous story) remained standing still where a strong punishment had seized her, because she would not obey the words of the thegns of glory.

Then Abraham went off alone at early dawn, so that he stood again where he, the wise patriarch, had earlier spoken in words with his Ruler. He saw a deadly smoke rising from the earth and flying far and wide.

Pride and wine-drinking had come upon them, so that they became too bold in wicked deeds, daring in sins; they forgot truth, the Lord's judgments, and who had given them prosperity and glory in their cities. Therefore the Prince of angels sent them surging-hot flame as punishment.
There the blessed Lot, faithful to his covenant and dear to the Ruler, lived for a great number of days, and his two daughters with him.
The women became pregnant; the willing sisters brought children into the world, sons of their old father.
Then the eternal Lord, our Saviour, helped him there, as he often did. He came himself by night to where the ruler lay drunk with wine.
Then the true King began to speak through a dream to the prince and angrily threatened him: "You have taken Abraham's woman, the bride from her husband.
"Lo, Lord of angels, will you ever in your anger take the life of, and cut down [?], one who lives here by right customs, is firm in counsel and in mind, and seeks mercy from you?

You, a foreigner, wished to ensnare us with deceit in this nation and to defile us with sins. You said in words that Sarah was your sister, your kinswoman by blood. Hatefully, you wished to bring guilt upon me through that woman, an immense evil.
Therefore I told the warriors in words that Sarah was my sister, everywhere on earth where the two of us, without a homeland, had to struggle among foreigners.
Then Abimelech began to enrich Abraham with worldly treasures and gave him back his wife.
Abraham did as his Lord commanded him and, at the Lord's bidding, accepted friendship with love and favours. He was dear to God.
Therefore he lived blessed in peace and went under the shadow of his Creator, covered by sheltering wings, while he lived here.
A child was born to Abraham from his bride. The Prince of angels had named him Isaac before the mother was pregnant with that offspring by her husband.
Ishmael shall never share the inheritance with Isaac, with my own child, after you are gone, when you send the life out of your body."

Afterwards the blessed son of Terah, the man of the Hebrews, was settled for a long time among the people of the Philistines, poor among strangers. The Lord of angels showed him a dwelling place, which the city-dwellers call the land of Beersheba.
When you have climbed a steep hill, the ridge of the high land that I will show you from here, going up on your own feet, there you shall prepare a pyre,
He did not delay the journey but at once began to hurry to set out. The word of the Lord of angels was awe-inspiring to him, and his Ruler was dear to him.

Then the blessed Abraham left his night's rest. He did not scorn the Saviour's command at all. The holy man girded himself with a grey sword, and showed that fear of the Guardian of spirits dwelt in his breast.
Then the old-hearted giver of gold began to bridle his asses, and he ordered two young men to travel with him.
His own kinsman was the third, and he himself the fourth. Then he set out eagerly from his own dwelling, leading Isaac, the ungrown child, as the Creator had commanded him.
Then he hurried greatly and pressed forward along the road, as the Lord had shown him the ways across the wilderness, until the glory-bright dawn of the third day rose up over the deep water.
Then the blessed man saw a high mountain towering, as the Lord of heaven had told him before.
Then Abraham spoke to his servants: "My men, rest here, the two of you, at this camp. The two of us will come back once we have carried out our errand to the King of spirits."
Then the prince and his own son went to the place that the Lord had shown him, making their way through the forests. The son carried the wood, the father the fire and the sword.
Then the man young in years began to ask Abraham about this: "My lord, we two have fire and a sword here. Where is the offering that you mean to bring to God, the bright one, as a burnt offering?"
Abraham spoke (he had firmly resolved to do as the Lord had commanded him): "The true King, the Guardian of mankind, will find that for himself, as seems fitting to him."

Then the resolute man climbed up the steep mountain with his son, as the Eternal One had commanded him, so that he stood on the summit of the high land, in the place that the strong and faithful Lord had shown him in words.

Then he began to build the pyre and kindle the fire. He fettered the feet and hands of his child, lifted young Isaac onto the pyre, and quickly grasped the sword by the hilt. He meant to kill his son with his own hands and give the fire his kinsman's blood to drink.
Then the Lord's servant, one of the angels from above, called to Abraham in a loud voice. He waited quietly for the messenger's words and answered the angel.

Then God's glorious spirit quickly spoke to him in words from the heavens above: "Dear Abraham, do not kill your own child, but take the boy, your son, alive from the pyre! The God of glory favours him!
Man of the Hebrews, you yourself shall receive rewards by the hand of the holy one, the King of heaven: true rewards of victory and ample gifts.
The Guardian of spirits will repay you graciously, because his friendship and favour were dearer to you than your own child."
The pyre stood kindled. The Creator of mankind had gladdened the heart of Abraham, kinsman of Lot, when he gave him back his child, Isaac, alive.
Then the blessed man, the warrior, looked over his shoulder and saw a ram standing there alone, not far away, the brother of Aaron [?], caught fast in brambles.
Abraham took it and lifted it onto the pyre with great haste in place of his own son.

Then he drew the blade and sprinkled the burnt offering, the smoking [?] altar, with the ram's blood. He sacrificed that offering to God and gave thanks for the rewards and for all the blessings that the Lord of gifts had granted him, later and earlier.
